paras: The attempted lynching of Adam Hunt took place at Roxboro, Person County, North Carolina, on the night of November 15, 1903, when forty or fifty men demanded the jail keys from Sheriff Thompson in order to lynch Hunt, a Black sawmill worker accused of killing the merchant Fleet Wilkins. The sheriff convinced the crowd that he did not have the keys, and it left without Hunt. Hunt was convicted within days and, after the state Supreme Court affirmed the verdict, hanged at Roxboro on June 15, 1904, an outcome the Richmond Times-Dispatch held up as justice that prevented lynching.

Hunt worked at the sawmill of R. W. Massic & Co. near Roxboro, where Wilkins's brother was bookkeeper and cashier. According to a Roxboro dispatch of November 9, Hunt demanded money at Wilkins's store, returned drunk when refused the balance, and beat him while Mrs. Wilkins tried to shoot Hunt with an unloaded pistol. A posse captured Hunt, and an Associated Press dispatch reported that Wilkins died on November 12.

According to L. J. Winstead, a visitor quoted in a Durham dispatch to the Raleigh News and Observer, some fifty men went to the sheriff's home soon after midnight and demanded the keys. The sheriff had given the keys to a deputy and persuaded the crowd that he had no access to the jail, and the men left. Congressman W. W. Kitchin, J. A. Long and others gathered to "use their influence to prevent a lynching in the county," but the crowd did not return.
A second dispatch said the would-be lynchers could find no one to lead them in a storm on the jail.

As court opened at Roxboro, two deputies kept Hunt overnight in the Durham jail for safety and returned him for trial. He was indicted, tried and sentenced to hang, on December 29 by the News and Observer's account. He appealed, arguing that the evidence of premeditation was insufficient, and was again moved to Durham; the Supreme Court affirmed in April 1904.

A Durham dispatch of April 13 said there had been "a demonstration against Hunt's life" after his conviction. He was hanged at Roxboro on June 15, 1904, after the governor declined to commute the sentence, and read a letter of warning to his race on the gallows. No report of arrests or charges against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

All known coverage came from white newspapers, chiefly the Raleigh News and Observer. Its "ATTEMPT TO LYNCH" story called Hunt "the negro who killed the young man Wilkins" before his trial, and the Clinton Caucasian reprinted it. The next day's headline credited Hunt's survival to the mob's lack of a leader.

The Associated Press report of Wilkins's death ran on November 13 in Richmond, Birmingham, Montgomery and Savannah. The Times-Dispatch closed its notice of the sentence with "This is the kind of justice to prevent lynching." At the hanging it called Hunt "a most desperate negro" and welcomed that "mob violence had not been resorted to."

The first Roxboro dispatch placed the beating inside the store, while the Times-Dispatch in 1904 said Hunt overtook Wilkins near his own door. The Supreme Court report printed the victim's name as "Fleetwood Williams." Reports placed the store two or three miles from Roxboro. Hunt reportedly said he had not meant to kill Wilkins, while the State was said to have evidence he had predicted a death that day.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Adam Hunt
bases: A crowd of forty or fifty men sought the jail keys to take Hunt from jail and lynch him, but left without him (A6, A7).

The crowd of forty or fifty men acted without authority to lynch Hunt for the killing of Wilkins, but did not get the keys and Hunt was not harmed (A6, A7); he was later executed by the state after conviction and appeal (A12, A15).

Two separate Durham dispatches to the News and Observer, the second with its own details, report the attempt (A6, A7), and a later Durham report and the Times-Dispatch's execution story refer to mob danger to Hunt (A13, A14); no report denies it.

framing.detail: The News and Observer headlined 'ATTEMPT TO LYNCH' and reported local efforts to prevent it, while calling Hunt 'the negro who killed' Wilkins before his trial.

The Times-Dispatch closed its sentence notice with 'This is the kind of justice to prevent lynching' and at the hanging called Hunt 'a most desperate negro' while welcoming that mob violence was avoided.
The AP report of Wilkins's death ran in Richmond, Birmingham, Montgomery and Savannah under headlines such as 'Was Beaten to Death.'
